why-react.name: What is React, and why does it exist?
why-react.desc: Updating the DOM by hand gets slow, tedious, and error-prone as an app grows. React solves this with a component model: you describe what the UI should look like, and React works out how to update the DOM efficiently. Facebook open-sourced it in 2013.
why-react.q: What problem does React solve? What was wrong with updating the DOM manually?
why-react.qsub: What is the difference between React and React DOM? Why are they separate packages?
why-react.what:
Definition: React is a JavaScript library for building user interfaces. Its core idea fits in one line: UI = f(state). You change the state, and React makes the screen match it.

In vanilla JS, you update the DOM by hand. In React, you only change the data.
why-react.analogy: Ordering at a restaurant. Imperative is walking into the kitchen and saying "turn on the gas, heat the oil, chop the onions." Declarative is telling the waiter "one paneer tikka, please." How it gets made is the chef's job.
why-react.why: As an app grows, manual DOM updates get harder and harder to manage. Say one piece of data appears in five places. When it changes, you have to update all five, and if you miss one, the UI and the data drift apart. This "state desync" bug is the most common one in manual DOM code. React rules this out by design, because the UI is always derived from the state.
pros: State desync bugs are practically eliminated
Components are reusable: write once, use in 20 places
The largest ecosystem and job market
cons: It is only a UI library, so routing and data fetching must be added separately
The bundle is larger than vanilla JS
Overkill for a small static site
gotchas: React is a library, not a framework. Unlike Angular, it doesn't ship with everything built in
The Virtual DOM exists to make declarative code possible, not simply to be "fast"
React builds the UI from state, so manipulating the DOM directly behind its back will confuse it
terms: you say "the screen should look like this" and React decides how to get there
you spell out every step: grab this element, change this text, remove this class
the UI is the output of a function whose input is the state
where: one piece of data appears in many widgets
validation, previews, and button state update on every keystroke
chat and notifications: data keeps arriving and the UI stays in sync
why-react.visualCap: Vanilla JS vs React: same task, different approach

setup.name: Setting up a React project: Vite, create-react-app, or Next.js
setup.desc: Vite: npm create vite@latest my-app -- --template react gives you the fastest setup. CRA: npx create-react-app my-app is older, slower, and deprecated. Next.js: npx create-next-app@latest is for SSR and full-stack apps. To learn React basics, use Vite.
setup.q: How do you create a new React project? What role does a bundler like Vite or webpack play?
setup.qsub: What does a bundler actually do? Why do you need one, and why can't you just write React in a plain .html file?
setup.what:
Definition: There are three common ways to start a React project: Vite (fast and simple, ideal for SPAs), Next.js (routing, SSR, and backend included), and CRA (create-react-app, now deprecated, so don't use it).

In 2026, use Vite for learning and SPAs, and Next.js for production websites and products.
setup.why: Browsers don't understand JSX or TypeScript, and they can't resolve package-style import statements. A build tool transforms all of this into plain JavaScript the browser can run, and bundles it for production. In development, Vite serves native ES modules, so its server starts in well under a second, where CRA could take 30 seconds or more.
pros: Vite's dev server starts almost instantly
Next.js gives you routing, image optimization, and SSR out of the box
Both support TypeScript out of the box
cons: Next.js has a steeper learning curve (server vs client components)
The many configuration files can be confusing at first
The ecosystem moves fast, so tutorials go out of date quickly
gotchas: create-react-app is dead. Skip any CRA tutorial written before 2023
In Vite, environment variables must start with VITE_ or they will be undefined
Don't commit node_modules. It belongs in .gitignore
terms: makes your files runnable in the browser (Vite, webpack)
Hot Module Replacement: the browser updates instantly when you save a file, with no full reload
a framework built on top of React that includes routing and SSR (Next.js)
where: Next.js: when you need SEO, routing, and an API

first-component.name: Your first React component: Hello World
first-component.desc:
A React component is just a JavaScript function that returns JSX. function App() { return

Hello World

; } is a complete component. React renders it into the DOM with createRoot(document.getElementById("root")).render().
first-component.q: What is a React component? How does React turn a component into actual HTML on the page?
first-component.qsub: What is the "root" element in index.html? How does React know where to mount your app?
first-component.what:
Definition: A React component is a plain JavaScript function that returns JSX. There is one naming rule: the name must start with a capital letter.

function Button() is a component. function button() is treated as an HTML tag, and it breaks.
first-component.analogy: A Lego brick. Build a brick (a component) once, then place it in 50 spots. Each brick has its own shape and snaps together with the others.
first-component.why: Components are React's unit of reuse. Build a <Card> once and use it in 30 places. When the design changes, you edit one file and all 30 places update. Each component also keeps its logic, markup, and styling together instead of spreading them across three separate files.
pros: Write it once, use it anywhere
Markup, logic, and style live together, so they're easy to find
Easy to test: it's just a function
cons: Too many tiny components can turn the file structure into a jungle
It takes practice to know when to split a component
gotchas: Start the name with a capital letter, or React will treat it as an HTML tag
A component can return only one root element. For two siblings, wrap them in a <>...</> fragment
Don't put the JSX on a new line right after return. JavaScript inserts a semicolon automatically. Wrap it in parentheses
terms: the DOM element where the entire React app is rendered
running a component so React knows what to show on screen
where: all of React is built from this one idea
Button, Input, and Card are all components
Header, Sidebar, and Footer are components too

what-is-jsx.name: What is JSX? HTML-like syntax inside JavaScript
what-is-jsx.desc:
JSX looks like HTML, but it's really JavaScript. Babel compiles

Hello

into React.createElement("h1", null, "Hello"). Rules: className instead of class, camelCase attributes (onClick, not onclick), and every tag must be closed (

what-is-jsx.q: What is JSX? Is it valid JavaScript? How does it work under the hood?
what-is-jsx.qsub: Why does React use className instead of class? What happens if you use class?
what-is-jsx.what:
Definition: JSX is a syntax extension for JavaScript that looks like HTML. Browsers don't understand it. During the build, it is transformed into React.createElement(...) calls (into jsx() calls in React 17+).

In other words, JSX is syntax sugar. Under the hood, you are just writing function calls.
what-is-jsx.analogy: An emoji. You see 😀, but inside the computer it's just a number (U+1F600). It looks different on the surface, but underneath it's something else.
what-is-jsx.why: Writing nested UI without JSX is painful: four levels of nesting means four nested createElement calls. With JSX, the same code reads like HTML. And because it's still JavaScript, you can use map, ternaries, and variables right inside it.
pros: Nested UI reads like HTML
The full power of JS is available: map, ternaries, variables
Typos are caught at compile time
cons: A build step is required
Small differences from HTML (className, htmlFor) can be confusing
Complex conditional logic gets messy inside JSX

A JSX comment is {/* like this */}, not // like this

props-state-intro.name: Props vs State: passing data and managing change
props-state-intro.desc: Props are data passed FROM a parent TO a child. They're read-only, like function parameters. State is data that lives INSIDE a component, and when it changes, React re-renders the component. Props are for configuration; state is for things that change. function Counter() { const [count, setCount] = useState(0); return <button onClick={() => setCount(c => c+1)}>{count}</button>; }
props-state-intro.q: What is the difference between props and state in React?
props-state-intro.qsub: What does it mean that props are immutable? What happens if you try to modify them directly?
props-state-intro.what:
Definition: React has two kinds of data:

  • Props come from outside, like function arguments. They are read-only.
  • State lives inside a component and is created with useState. It can change, and when it does, the UI updates.

A one-line rule: if it changes, it belongs in state; if it doesn't, it's a prop.
props-state-intro.analogy: Props are your birth name: your parents gave it to you and you can't change it yourself. State is your mood: it belongs to you, it changes all the time, and when it changes, your expression changes too.
props-state-intro.why: This split creates a one-way data flow: data always moves from top to bottom. When the UI looks wrong, you can walk up the tree to find where the data came from. If a child could change its parent's data, tracing a bug would become nearly impossible.
pros: Data flows in one direction, so debugging is easier
Components that use only props are pure: the same props always produce the same output
Keeping state in one place gives you a single source of truth
cons: In a deep tree, props may have to pass through five levels (prop drilling)
Beginners find it hard to decide which data should be state
gotchas: Never mutate props. They are read-only, and mutating them causes bugs that fail silently
Don't create state for values you can derive from props (total = price × qty shouldn't be state)
setState doesn't change the value immediately. The new value is available on the next render
terms: data passed from parent to child; the child cannot change it
a component's own data that can change; changing it triggers a re-render
the component function runs again to produce new UI
where: this is React's most basic mental model
the input's value is state; the label text is a prop
the items live in state in the parent, and each row receives them as props
props-state-intro.visualCap: Data flows down, events flow up

jsx.name: JSX & React.createElement
jsx.desc: JSX is syntactic sugar. Babel compiles it into React.createElement() calls that return plain JS objects called React Elements.
jsx.q: What does JSX actually compile to? What is the difference between a React Element and a React Component?
jsx.qsub: Why can't you return two sibling elements without a wrapper? What problem does Fragment solve?
jsx.what:
Definition: JSX compiles into a function call that returns a plain object. That object is a "React Element": a description of what should appear on screen, not an actual DOM node.

Before React 17, the compiler produced React.createElement calls, so import React was required. With the automatic runtime in React 17+, the compiler imports jsx for you.
jsx.why: Understanding this matters for two reasons. First, writing JSX is cheap: it only creates an object and never touches the DOM directly. Second, <Foo /> does not execute Foo. It only creates a description of it, and React decides when to run it.
pros: Creating an Element is very cheap, with no DOM operations
Elements are immutable objects, so React can safely compare them
In React 17+, you no longer need to import React
cons: There is an extra layer of abstraction to understand
Older tutorials show the classic runtime, which can cause confusion
gotchas: <Foo /> does not call Foo(). It only creates an object
In development, elements are frozen, so assigning el.props.x = 1 won't work (it throws in strict mode, which ES modules use)
If the type is a string, it's a DOM tag; if it's a function, it's a component. That's why the capital-letter rule exists

vdom.name: Virtual DOM
vdom.desc: An in-memory tree of JS objects that mirrors the real DOM. React diffs the new tree against the old one and applies only the minimal changes to the real DOM.
vdom.q: What is the Virtual DOM, and why does React use it? Does it always make things faster?
vdom.qsub: What is the actual cost of the Virtual DOM? When would direct DOM manipulation be faster?
vdom.what: Definition: The Virtual DOM is a lightweight JavaScript representation of the real DOM. When state changes, React builds a new virtual tree, compares it with the old one, and applies only what changed to the real DOM.
vdom.analogy: A house blueprint. Before knocking down a wall, you draw a new blueprint, compare it with the old one, and demolish only the wall that has to change. You don't tear down the whole house.
vdom.why:
DOM operations are expensive, because each change can trigger layout and paint. If React rebuilt the whole DOM on every state change, the app would stall. Instead, diffing happens on plain JavaScript objects (cheap), and only a minimal set of updates reaches the DOM (expensive, but few).

The honest truth: the Virtual DOM is not faster than carefully hand-optimized DOM code. It is "fast enough" while letting you write declarative code. Speed isn't the main point; developer experience is.
pros: You write declarative code and React handles the optimization
Diffing happens in JavaScript, so DOM operations are kept to a minimum
It's cross-platform: the same concept powers React Native
cons: It uses extra memory, since two trees must be kept
It is slower than carefully optimized vanilla JavaScript
Svelte and SolidJS skip this layer and are faster
gotchas: The Virtual DOM isn't there to be "fast"; it makes declarative coding possible
If an element's type changes, React doesn't reuse the node, and the state of the whole subtree is lost
React 19 still uses a virtual DOM. Fiber is how it is implemented, not a replacement

comparing the old and new trees to find the differences
applying the minimal set of changes to the real DOM based on the diff

class-vs-functional.name: Class vs Functional Components
class-vs-functional.desc: Class components use lifecycle methods and this; functional components use hooks. Hooks give functions everything classes could do, and more.
class-vs-functional.q: What are the key differences between class and functional components? Why did the React team move to hooks?
class-vs-functional.qsub: Is there anything class components can do that functional components still can't fully replicate?
class-vs-functional.what:
Definition: React components used to be written in two ways. Class components (the standard before hooks arrived in 2019) rely on this.state, this.setState, and lifecycle methods. Functional components (the standard today) get the same capabilities from hooks, without this.

New code is always functional. Classes appear only in legacy code and in Error Boundaries.
class-vs-functional.why: In a class, the logic for a single task was split across three lifecycle methods: subscribe in componentDidMount, update in componentDidUpdate, and clean up in componentWillUnmount. With hooks, all three live in a single useEffect. Custom hooks also removed the "wrapper hell" of HOCs and render props that was used to share logic.
pros: Less code and no this headaches
Logic is easy to reuse with custom hooks
Related logic stays in one place instead of being scattered across lifecycle methods
cons: Hooks have their own rules (call them only at the top level)
Stale closures introduce a new class of bugs
Classes are still required for Error Boundaries
gotchas: Error Boundaries can only be written as classes. This is a favorite interview question
In classes, this.setState merges state; useState replaces it
A functional component re-runs the whole function on every render, so local variables are recreated
terms: the old way: class extends React.Component with a render() method
the current standard: a plain function plus hooks
a class's special methods, such as componentDidMount and componentDidUpdate
where: still needs a class; there is no hook equivalent
you should be able to read old class components
class-vs-functional.visualCap: Same logic: scattered in a class, unified in a hook

props.name: Props & Immutability
props.desc: Props are read-only inputs that flow from parent to child. Mutating props directly breaks the one-way data flow contract.
props.q: Why are props immutable? What happens to child components when a parent re-renders?
props.qsub: What is prop drilling, and what are the solutions? When is prop drilling actually fine?
props.what: Definition: Props are the data a parent passes to a child. React treats them as read-only, so a child cannot change its props. React's rule: "every component should behave like a pure function with respect to its props."
props.why: Immutability matters because React compares by reference (Object.is). If you mutate an object in place, the reference stays the same, React concludes nothing changed, and the UI doesn't update. That's why you should always create a new object or array.
pros: Components are predictable: same props, same UI
Reference comparison lets React diff quickly
Composition with children is very flexible
cons: Every update creates a new object, which produces some garbage
Spread chains get long for deeply nested updates
Prop drilling becomes painful in deep trees
gotchas: sort(), reverse(), splice(), and push() all mutate the ORIGINAL array. Make a copy first
Inline object/array props ({} or []) create a new reference on every render, which breaks memoization
Put your own props before the spread, so callers can override your defaults

passing all props at once with {...obj}
where: the standard way to pass data down

state-basics.name: State & Re-renders
state-basics.desc: State is private, mutable data. Changing it schedules a re-render, and React batches state updates for efficiency.
state-basics.q: What triggers a re-render in React? What does NOT trigger one?
state-basics.qsub: If you call setState with the same value as the current state, does React re-render?
state-basics.what:
Definition: State is a component's private data. It persists across re-renders, and changing it makes React re-render. const [x, setX] = useState(initial).

Two important truths: (1) setX does not change the value immediately; the new value appears on the next render. (2) React batches all the setState calls from one event into a single re-render.
state-basics.analogy: A photo. Each render is a photo that captures the values at that moment. Calling setX orders a new photo, but the one in your hand is still the old one.
state-basics.why: Without this understanding, you hit the classic bug: calling setCount(count+1) three times adds 1, not 3, because each call reads count from the same old snapshot. With a functional update, setCount(c => c+1), React hands you the latest value each time, so you get +3.
pros: Batching turns one event into one render, which is good for performance
Functional updates avoid stale-value bugs
Lazy initialization runs an expensive initial calculation only once
cons: The asynchronous behavior confuses beginners a lot
Object and array state must be copied manually
When you have many related useState hooks, useReducer is a better fit
gotchas: Reading the value right after setState gives you the OLD value. This is by design, not a bug
Anything that depends on the previous value should use a functional update
useState(expensiveFn()) calls expensiveFn on every render. Write useState(() => expensiveFn()) instead
terms: the hook that creates state; it returns [value, setValue]
combining multiple setState calls into a single re-render
setX(prev => ...): computes the new value from the previous one
where: API data plus loading and error flags

keys.name: Keys in Lists
keys.desc: Keys help React identify which items in a list changed, were added, or were removed. They are critical for correct reconciliation.
keys.q: Why does React need keys? What happens if you use the index as a key? When is an index key actually safe?
keys.qsub: What is key remounting? When would you deliberately change a key to reset a component?
keys.what: Definition: A key is a special prop that tells React which item is the same item across two renders of a list. Without keys, React matches items by position, which goes wrong when items are added, removed, or reordered.
keys.analogy: A roll number in a class. If you identify students by position (first, second) and one leaves from the middle, everyone's identity shifts. A roll number (the key) prevents that.
keys.why: Keys are not just about silencing a warning. Getting them wrong causes real bugs. Say you insert an item at the top of a list that uses index keys. React sees a new item at position 0, assumes "it's the same old item with different text," and reuses the DOM node. The result: text typed into an input ends up in the wrong row, and a checkbox stays ticked on the wrong item.
pros: React tracks items correctly, so DOM nodes and state stay in the right place
On a reorder, React moves nodes instead of recreating them
Changing a key is a clean trick for resetting a component
cons: Without a stable id, producing a key is difficult
A Math.random() key remounts on every render, which is very slow
Wrong-key bugs are very confusing to track down
gotchas: A key only needs to be unique among siblings, not globally
You can't read the key from props: props.key is undefined, because React keeps it internally
Never write key={Math.random()}. Every render gets a new key, so the whole list remounts
terms: a unique identifier given to each item in a list
using the array position (0, 1, 2) as the key; often wrong
the component is replaced with a brand-new one, and all its internal state is lost

controlled-uncontrolled.name: Controlled vs Uncontrolled Components
controlled-uncontrolled.desc: Controlled: React state owns the input's value. Uncontrolled: the DOM owns it, and you read it through a ref. Both have legitimate use cases.
controlled-uncontrolled.q: What is the difference between controlled and uncontrolled inputs? When would you use each?
controlled-uncontrolled.qsub: What is the difference between defaultValue and value on a React input, and what goes wrong if you mix them up?
controlled-uncontrolled.what:
Definition: There are two ways to handle a form input:

  • Controlled uses value={state} plus onChange. React always holds the source of truth.
  • Uncontrolled uses defaultValue plus a ref. The DOM holds the truth, and React reads it only when needed, such as on submit.
controlled-uncontrolled.analogy: Controlled is like asking your manager for approval before every word you say. Uncontrolled is like doing the work yourself and reporting back in the meeting.
controlled-uncontrolled.why: Controlled is the default because you get control on every keystroke: live validation, a character counter, input formatting (such as dashes in phone numbers), and disabling other fields. Uncontrolled inputs are fast because they don't re-render, but they can't do any of that.
pros: Controlled: full control, with live validation, formatting, and dependent fields
Uncontrolled: no re-render on each keystroke, which is fast for large forms
React Hook Form gives you the best of both
cons: Controlled: a 30-field form re-renders on every keystroke, which can be slow
Uncontrolled: the value isn't in React state, so dependent logic is harder
Mixing the two leads to confusing bugs
gotchas: If you pass a value without onChange, the input becomes read-only. Use readOnly or defaultValue instead
If a value goes from undefined to a string, React warns about switching from uncontrolled to controlled. Always initialize with an empty string ""
File inputs can't be controlled, for browser security reasons

the input keeps its own value in the DOM, and React reads it through a ref
the initial value of an uncontrolled input
where: React Hook Form uses uncontrolled inputs, which is why it's fast

strictmode.name: StrictMode
strictmode.desc: A development-only tool that double-invokes render functions and effects to surface side-effect bugs and deprecated API usage.
strictmode.q: What does StrictMode do? Why does it call some functions twice in development?
strictmode.qsub: If StrictMode breaks your code by running effects twice, what does that reveal about your code?
strictmode.what:
Definition: <StrictMode> is a development-only wrapper. It renders nothing itself. It just tells React to "check extra strictly." The most visible effect: components render twice and effects run twice (mount, unmount, mount again).

In a production build, it does nothing at all.
strictmode.analogy: A fire drill. There's no fire, but the alarm is sounded on purpose to check that the evacuation route really works.
strictmode.why:
Future React features (such as Offscreen, or preserving state with Suspense) may unmount a component and mount it again. If your effect cleanup is wrong, say a timer isn't cleared or a subscription isn't removed, it will cause trouble later. StrictMode exposes that bug today.

Seeing an API call run twice is not a bug. It's StrictMode. Don't "fix" it with a ref guard; the real fix is to abort the request in the cleanup.
pros: Catches missing cleanup and impure renders early
Zero cost in production
Warns about deprecated APIs

fiber-arch.name: React Fiber Architecture
fiber-arch.desc: A complete rewrite of React's reconciler (React 16+). Fiber turns the render tree into a linked list of units of work that can be paused, aborted, and resumed.
fiber-arch.q: What is React Fiber, and why was it a complete rewrite? What problem does it solve compared with the old stack reconciler?
fiber-arch.qsub: What is a fiber node? What properties does it hold?
fiber-arch.what:
Definition: Fiber is the reconciliation engine in React 16+. For each component, React creates a fiber node: a plain object holding the component's type, props, state, and pointers to its parent, child, and sibling.

This turns recursion into a linked-list traversal, and a linked list can be paused halfway through. That is the whole point of Fiber.
fiber-arch.analogy: Reading a book. Recursion is reading the entire book in one sitting: if someone interrupts you, you have to start over. Fiber is using a bookmark: you pick up right where you stopped.
fiber-arch.why:
In React 15, reconciliation was recursive. Recursion uses the JavaScript call stack, and a call stack can't be paused halfway. A tree of 5,000 components could block the main thread for 200 ms or more, freezing the user's typing.

With Fiber, React can ask after each node, "Does the browser have any urgent work?" If so, it pauses, lets the browser run, then resumes from that point. This is what made useTransition, Suspense, and concurrent rendering possible.

A priority system becomes possible: urgent updates run first
An in-progress update can be dropped or restarted

The render function may run more than once, which breaks impure code
Debugging is harder
gotchas: Fiber does not replace the Virtual DOM. It is a way of implementing it
The render phase is interruptible, but the commit phase is NOT. Commit always completes in one go

reconciliation.name: Reconciliation & the Diffing Algorithm
reconciliation.desc: React's O(n) algorithm for comparing two trees, built on two heuristics: elements of different types produce different trees, and keys identify stable elements across renders.
reconciliation.q: Explain how React's diffing algorithm works. What are the two assumptions that make it O(n) instead of O(n³)?
reconciliation.qsub:
What happens in the diff when a parent changes from a
to a ? What about when you reorder list items with and without keys?
reconciliation.what:
Definition: Reconciliation is the algorithm that compares the old fiber tree with the new element tree. A perfect tree diff is O(n³): for 1,000 nodes, that's around a billion operations. React applies two heuristics to bring it down to O(n):

  1. A different type means a different tree. React doesn't compare them; it discards the old one and builds a new one.
  2. Items at the same level are matched by their key.
reconciliation.why:
These two rules are almost always true: nobody expects the same content after swapping a <div> for a <span>. In exchange, React does roughly a million times less work for a 1,000-node tree.

But there is a major side effect: changing the type discards the entire state of the subtree. This is the real cause of the "my input reset" bug.

DOM nodes are reused when the type is the same, so state is preserved
Lists are reordered efficiently with keys

If the type changes, the subtree's state silently disappears
You can't move a component between two positions in the tree and keep its state

Most "input reset" bugs come from this: the type or the key changed
React treats the same position and the same type as the SAME component, even if they're logically different

render-commit.name: Render Phase vs Commit Phase
render-commit.desc: Render phase: pure, interruptible work where React builds the new Fiber tree. Commit phase: synchronous and uninterruptible, where React applies DOM mutations and runs effects.
render-commit.q: What is the difference between the render phase and the commit phase? Why must the render phase be pure?
render-commit.qsub: In which phase do useEffect and useLayoutEffect run? Why does useLayoutEffect have to be synchronous?
render-commit.what:
Definition: Every update happens in two phases:

  • Render (thinking) — component functions run, a new tree is created, and diffing happens. Nothing touches the DOM. React can pause, restart, or throw away this work.
  • Commit (doing) — React updates the DOM, attaches refs, and runs effects. This happens in one go, without pausing.
render-commit.analogy: Drawing a house blueprint (render) vs. building the wall (commit). You can tear up and redraw the blueprint ten times at no cost. Once the wall is going up, you can't stop halfway.
render-commit.why:
This split explains a lot of React's behavior:

  • Don't run side effects during render. React may run a render twice or discard it, which is exactly why StrictMode double-invokes components.
  • useEffect runs after the commit (after the browser paints), which is why it feels asynchronous.
  • useLayoutEffect runs inside the commit, before the paint. That makes it right for DOM measurements, but it blocks painting.
pros: An interruptible render keeps the UI responsive
Commit is atomic, so the user never sees a half-finished UI
Effect timing is predictable
cons: The purity rule of the render phase is easy to break
Beginners mix up the two effect hooks
A long commit still blocks the main thread
gotchas: Don't read or write the DOM, fetch, or set timers during render
useLayoutEffect blocks painting, so use it only when you must measure the DOM before paint
Refs are attached during commit, so ref.current can be null during render

scheduler.name: React Scheduler & Priority Lanes
scheduler.desc: React's scheduler assigns each update a priority lane (SyncLane, InputContinuousLane, DefaultLane, IdleLane) and processes the highest-priority work first.
scheduler.q: How does React decide which updates to process first? What are lanes in React?
scheduler.qsub: How does startTransition use the scheduler to deprioritize an update?
scheduler.what:
Definition: The Scheduler is React's priority system. Every update gets a lane. More urgent lanes are processed first, and less urgent work waits.

Priority order, most urgent first: Sync (discrete events like click or keypress) → InputContinuous (hover, drag) → Default (normal setState) → Transition (startTransition) → Idle (offscreen).
scheduler.analogy: A hospital emergency room. A heart attack (click) is treated first, a fracture (hover) next, and a routine checkup (transition) waits. But even routine cases eventually get seen, so nobody waits forever (starvation protection).
scheduler.why: Without priorities, all work is equal, so filtering a large list could block typing. Lanes let React say "typing first, filtered list later" and interrupt the filtering work to show the keystroke. useTransition does exactly this.

work-loop.name: Work Loop & Time Slicing
work-loop.desc: The Fiber work loop processes one Fiber node at a time and yields back to the browser every ~5ms so frames aren't blocked, which makes rendering interruptible.
work-loop.q: What is time slicing in React? How does the work loop render without blocking the browser?
work-loop.qsub: What API does React use to yield back to the browser (MessageChannel, requestIdleCallback, etc.), and why?
work-loop.what: Definition: The work loop is React's main engine. It is a while loop that processes one fiber at a time and, after each fiber, asks: "Have my 5ms run out?" If so, it yields (lets the browser run) and resumes from the same spot later.
work-loop.analogy: Studying with a break every 25 minutes (Pomodoro). The work still gets done, but you don't turn into a machine, and everything else in your life keeps moving in between.
work-loop.why: The browser has about 16.6 ms per frame (60 fps). If React holds the thread for 200 ms, about 12 frames are dropped and the user thinks the app has hung. With 5 ms slices, React keeps working while the browser still gets to paint. The total work time stays the same, but the app feels responsive.

Low-priority work can be interrupted or discarded

batching.name: Batching (React 17 vs React 18)
batching.desc: React 17 batches state updates only inside React event handlers. React 18 batches ALL updates automatically, including those in setTimeout, promises, and native events.
batching.q: What is state batching? How does React 18's automatic batching differ from React 17? How do you opt out?
batching.qsub: What is flushSync and when would you need it?
batching.what:
Definition: Batching means combining all setState calls made in the same tick into a single re-render.

In React 17, batching happened only inside React event handlers. Inside setTimeout, promises, or native listeners, each setState triggered its own render. In React 18, batching happens everywhere. This is called “automatic batching”.
batching.why: Three setState calls would mean three renders: three full tree diffs and three DOM commits. Batching reduces that to one. In React 17, fetch().then(() => { setLoading(false); setData(d); }) caused two renders, so there was a frame where loading was false but the data hadn't arrived yet (a flash of empty state). In React 18 this bug disappears automatically.

You get it for free in React 18

element-component-instance.name: React Element vs Component vs Instance
element-component-instance.desc: Element: a plain object describing what to render. Component: a function or class that returns elements. Instance: the live record of a mounted component. Only class components expose one (this).
element-component-instance.q: What is the difference between a React element, a React component, and a React instance?
element-component-instance.qsub: Why don't function components have instances? What does that mean for refs?
element-component-instance.what:
Definition: Three different things that people often mix up:

  • Component = the recipe (the function Card)
  • Element = the order slip (<Card title="Hi"/>: just an object, nothing has run yet)
  • Instance = the actual dish (the fiber node that holds state, effects, and the DOM pointer)
element-component-instance.analogy: Recipe (component) → order slip (element) → plated dish (instance). One recipe can produce 100 order slips, and each order slip produces its own separate dish.
element-component-instance.why:
This distinction answers two common questions:

  • "Does creating an element run the component?" No. <Card/> only creates an object. React decides when to call Card().
  • "Where does state live?" Not in the component (it's just a function) and not in the element (it's immutable). It lives in the instance/fiber. So when the fiber is destroyed, the state disappears with it.

React manages state through the instance, so you don't have to
You can have any number of independent instances of the same component

rules-of-hooks.name: Rules of Hooks & Their Internals
rules-of-hooks.desc: Hooks must be called at the top level and only from React functions. React stores hook state in a linked list on the Fiber node, matched by call order.
rules-of-hooks.q: Why can't hooks be called inside conditionals or loops? What would break internally if you did?
rules-of-hooks.qsub: How does React know which useState call corresponds to which state value across re-renders?
rules-of-hooks.what:
Definition: Two rules:

  1. Call hooks only at the top level, never inside an if, a loop, or a nested function.
  2. Call them only from a React function component or a custom hook.

The reason in one line: React identifies hooks by order, not name.
rules-of-hooks.analogy: People standing in a line with no name tags. You can only tell who is who by counting: first, second, third. If the second person sometimes steps out of line, the third person is suddenly mistaken for the second.
rules-of-hooks.why: Inside a fiber, hooks are stored in a linked list. On each render, React walks the list from the start: the first useState call gets the first node, the second call gets the second node. If you put a hook inside an if and the condition turns false, everything after it shifts, and the state meant for name ends up read by age. React can't detect this at runtime, which is why the lint rule exists.

Hooks compose well because the call order is predictable
The lint rule catches most mistakes

useeffect.name: useEffect — Timing, Deps, Cleanup
useeffect.desc: Runs after paint, asynchronously. The dependency array controls when it re-runs. The cleanup function runs before the next effect and on unmount.

Definition: useEffect(fn, deps) tells React: "after the commit and paint, do this work." The deps array says when to run it again.

  • [a, b] → whenever a or b changes

usememo.name: useMemo — When to Use & When Not To
usememo.desc: Memoizes the result of an expensive computation and recalculates only when dependencies change. It costs memory and adds complexity, so it's only worth it for genuinely expensive work.
usememo.q: When should you use useMemo? What is the overhead of useMemo itself? When does it hurt performance?
usememo.qsub: Why is useMemo a performance hint rather than a semantic guarantee? React may discard memoized values. Does that matter?
usememo.what:
Definition: useMemo(fn, deps) remembers the result of a calculation. If the dependencies haven't changed, fn doesn't run again and the previous result is returned.

There are two valid reasons: (1) the calculation is truly expensive, and (2) you need a stable reference so downstream memo or effects don't break.
usememo.why:
The second reason is the more important one. const opts = {a:1} creates a new object on every render. If you pass it as a prop to a React.memo child, memoization becomes useless because the child re-renders every time. useMemo keeps the reference stable.

But don't memoize everything. useMemo has its own costs: dependency comparison and memory. Memoizing a simple a+b is wasteful. The React Compiler is starting to handle much of this automatically.

Reference stability keeps downstream memo chains working
Prevents infinite loops in effects
cons: It has its own cost: memory and dependency comparison
Incorrect deps cause silent stale-value bugs
Code gets harder to read
gotchas: Measure with the Profiler first, then memoize. Don't guess
useMemo is not a guarantee; React may discard the cache (for example, under memory pressure)
Memoization only helps when a new object or array would otherwise be passed as a prop on every render

optimizing without measuring, which is often harmful

usecallback.name: useCallback — Referential Stability
usecallback.desc: Returns a memoized function reference that changes only when its dependencies change. Critical when passing callbacks to memoized child components.
usecallback.q: Why does useCallback exist? When does it actually improve performance, and when is it wasted?
usecallback.qsub: If useCallback is just useMemo returning a function, when would you choose one over the other?
usecallback.what:
Definition: useCallback(fn, deps) is equivalent to useMemo(() => fn, deps). It remembers the function so you get the same reference on every render.

In JavaScript, every render creates a new function object for () => {}. It looks identical, but the reference is different. That defeats a child wrapped in React.memo.
usecallback.why:
useCallback on its own is useless. It pays off only when the receiver cares about the reference: the child is wrapped in React.memo, the function is a dependency of an effect, or it is passed into a custom hook.

If the child isn't memoized, adding useCallback only adds cost with zero benefit.

usereducer.name: useReducer — Complex State Logic
usereducer.desc: An alternative to useState for complex state transitions. Takes (state, action) => newState, which keeps state logic testable and in one place.
usereducer.q: When would you choose useReducer over useState? Implement a cart with useReducer.
usereducer.qsub: How does useReducer + useContext compare to Redux? When would you still reach for Redux?
usereducer.what:
Definition: useReducer(reducer, initial) — when several state values are related, keep them in a single reducer instead of separate useState calls. Every change is described as an "action".

Rule of thumb: 3+ related pieces of state, or one event that changes several of them → use useReducer.
usereducer.analogy: A bank. You don't change the balance directly. You fill out a form (an action) like “withdraw 1000”, and the bank's rules (the reducer) validate it and produce a new balance. Every transaction is recorded.
usereducer.why:
With separate useState calls, you have to write "loading true, error null, data null" by hand everywhere, and forgetting one spot creates an impossible state (e.g., loading and error both true). In a reducer, each transition is defined in one place, so invalid combinations can't occur.

Bonus: the dispatch reference is always stable, so it's safe to include in dependency arrays.

usecontext.name: useContext — Performance Trap
usecontext.desc: Subscribes a component to the nearest context value. Every change to the context value re-renders ALL consumers, even those that use only part of it.
usecontext.q: What is the performance problem with useContext? How do you prevent unnecessary re-renders from context changes?
usecontext.qsub: What patterns split a context to avoid over-rendering? How does Zustand solve this differently?
usecontext.what:
Definition: Context is a way to avoid prop drilling. A Provider supplies a value, and anywhere below it in the tree you can read that value with useContext.

Performance trap: when the context value changes, all consumers re-render, even if they only use a small part of it.
usecontext.analogy: Home WiFi. You don't have to run a cable to every room (prop drilling). But if you change the WiFi password, every device disconnects, even the ones that didn't care.
usecontext.why:
The most common bug is <Ctx.Provider value={{ user, setUser }}>. That object is new on every render, so every consumer re-renders whenever the parent renders, even if the user hasn't changed. Fix: memoize the value with useMemo.

Another fix is to split the context: put frequently changing data in one context and stable values (like functions) in another. Components that only use the functions then won't re-render when the data changes.

Easy to test by swapping the Provider
Built in, so no extra library is needed
cons: Every value change re-renders all consumers
No selectors, so you can't subscribe to a slice of the value
A poor fit for rapidly changing data (Zustand/Jotai are better)

Don't treat context as a state manager; it's a dependency-injection tool
Don't put rapidly changing data (mouse position, form values) in context

Definition: A custom hook is a normal function that (a) starts with use and (b) calls other hooks inside. It lets you pull stateful logic out of a component and reuse it.

state-decision.qsub: What is the difference between server state and client state? Why does that distinction matter?
state-decision.what:
Definition: Where state lives is a decision, not a default. The most important question is: is this server data or client data?

  • Client state → useState, kept as low in the tree as possible.
  • Derived data → don't create state; calculate it during render.

redux.what:
Definition: Redux is a predictable state container built on three rules: (1) a single store, (2) state is read-only, so you can only change it by dispatching actions, and (3) changes are made by pure reducers.

Data flows in one direction: dispatch(action) → middleware → reducer → naya state → UI.
redux.analogy: A court's record room. Nobody edits a file directly. You submit a request (the action), the clerk (the reducer) follows the rules to write a new record, and the old record stays on file so you can trace what happened.
redux.why:
The real benefit of Redux is traceability. DevTools shows every action and every state change, which enables time-travel debugging. In a large team with a complex app, you can answer “who changed this state?” in seconds.

But today, don't write plain Redux. Use Redux Toolkit, and don't use Redux for server data. Use React Query for that.

code-splitting.desc: React.lazy() enables dynamic import() for components. Suspense shows a fallback while the chunk loads. This reduces the initial bundle size and time to interactive (TTI).

concurrent-mode.what:
Definition: Concurrent React means React can pause, resume or discard a render. It isn't a feature you switch "on". It's a capability that comes with createRoot, and you use it through useTransition/useDeferredValue/Suspense.

It is not parallel. JavaScript is still single-threaded; this is just smarter scheduling.
concurrent-mode.analogy: One cook, two orders. He doesn't cook both at once, but if an urgent order comes in, he pauses the slower dish, handles the urgent one, then goes back to the first.
concurrent-mode.why: In older React, once a render started it had to finish. While a heavy list rendered, your typing would freeze. In concurrent React, React decides that typing matters more: it throws away the half-finished list render, shows the typed text, then resumes the list.

Priority-based updates
Suspense and streaming SSR are built on it

There's a new mental model to learn
Incorrect usage can make the UI feel laggy

suspense.qsub: What is the difference between "fetch-then-render" and "render-as-you-fetch"? How does Suspense enable the latter?
suspense.what:
Definition: <Suspense fallback={...}> is a boundary. If any component inside it is "not ready yet" (a lazy chunk is loading, or data is still arriving), React shows the fallback, and then the real content once it's ready.

This moves the loading state from inside each component to the tree structure.
suspense.analogy: A placeholder plate at a restaurant. The plate (the fallback) stays on the table until the food arrives, so the table never looks empty. When the food comes, the placeholder is removed.
suspense.why:
Without Suspense, each component had to write if (loading) return <Spinner/>. Ten components meant ten separate spinners and a flickering page. With Suspense, you decide in one place what the loading UI for a whole section looks like.

Important: a plain useEffect fetch does not trigger Suspense. You need a Suspense-enabled source: React Query (suspense mode), RSC, a framework loader, or use().

Granular control with nested boundaries
Reduces waterfalls by letting fetches run in parallel

Errors need a separate ErrorBoundary

The higher the boundary, the more of the page falls back. Use smaller boundaries

usetransition.qsub: What is the difference between useTransition and debouncing? When would you use each?

Definition: const [isPending, startTransition] = useTransition(). React treats state updates inside startTransition(fn) as non-urgent. If an urgent update arrives, React pauses them, or discards and restarts them.

usedeferredvalue.q: What is the difference between useDeferredValue and useTransition? When would you reach for one over the other?

streaming-ssr.desc: React 18's renderToPipeableStream sends HTML as it becomes ready. Selective hydration lets React hydrate the part the user is interacting with first.

Definition: Classic SSR is all-or-nothing: the server sends nothing until all the data for the whole page has arrived. With streaming SSR, the server sends whatever is ready immediately and streams the remaining chunks later, based on your Suspense boundaries.

hoc.desc: A function that takes a component and returns an enhanced component. It was the classic reuse pattern before hooks and has largely been replaced by custom hooks.
hoc.what:
Definition: A Higher-Order Component (HOC) is a function of the shape Component → Component. It takes an existing component, wraps it with extra props or behavior, and returns a new component.

compound-components.q: What is the compound component pattern? Build a Tabs component with it.
compound-components.qsub: What is the difference between implicit state sharing (Context) and explicit prop passing in compound components?
compound-components.what: Definition: A parent component shares its state with its children through context. The user writes <Tabs><Tabs.List><Tabs.Tab/></Tabs.List><Tabs.Panel/></Tabs>, much like HTML's <select>/<option>.

The alternative is a mountain of props: <Tabs items={[...]} renderTab={} renderPanel={} tabClass="" panelClass="" />. As requirements grow, the props keep multiplying and the component becomes unwieldy.

rtl-philosophy.what:
Definition: RTL has one guiding principle: "the more your tests resemble the way your software is used, the more confidence they can give you". So RTL doesn't touch state, props or internal functions. It only interacts with what is visible on the screen.

If you test implementation details, your tests break on every refactor, even when the app works perfectly. Those tests get in your way instead of helping. RTL tests survive refactors and fail only when something is genuinely broken.

Bonus: using getByRole also checks accessibility. If a button has no accessible name, the query fails.

Definition: Testing everything is wasteful. Test where the damage from a break is high:

nextjs-overview.what:

nextjs-hydration.what:
Definition: The server sends HTML that is rendered but not yet interactive. Then the JavaScript arrives and React attaches its component tree to that HTML and wires up the event handlers. This step is called hydration.

A mismatch happens when the client's first render differs from the server's HTML. React then discards the affected markup and re-renders it on the client, which causes flicker and wasted work.

Mismatches almost always come from the same few causes: Date.now(), Math.random(), window/localStorage access, timezone or locale differences, or a browser extension modifying the DOM.

The fix is simple: make the first client render identical to the server's output, and show browser-specific values from useEffect (that is, on the second render).

  • metadata export — SEO tags rendered on the server
  • next/script — control over how third-party scripts load
nextjs-optimisations.why: These features directly affect Core Web Vitals, which count toward Google ranking. An image without width/height causes CLS. Fonts loaded from the Google Fonts CDN add a DNS lookup, a new connection and FOUT. And metadata set on the client is never seen by crawlers.

nextjs-api-routes.q: When would you use API routes vs Server Actions? What are the trade-offs?
nextjs-api-routes.what:
Definition: Next.js gives you two ways to run code on the server:

  • Route Handler — create app/api/x/route.ts and export GET/POST functions from it. This is a real HTTP endpoint that mobile apps, webhooks and external clients can call.
  • Server Action — an async function marked 'use server' that you call directly from a form or button. Next.js handles the HTTP layer for you.
nextjs-api-routes.why:
A Server Action removes the boilerplate of “create an API route, write the fetch, manage loading state, handle errors”. The form even works without JavaScript (progressive enhancement), because it is a real HTML form submission.

You need a route handler when something outside your UI must call the endpoint: a webhook, a mobile app or a cron job.
pros: Almost no boilerplate with Server Actions
Forms work even without JavaScript
revalidatePath refreshes the cache instantly
cons: A Server Action is a public endpoint, so you must secure it yourself
Debugging is harder, since the calls are not obvious in the network tab
Only works with Next.js, so it is not portable
gotchas: A Server Action is a PUBLIC endpoint: do auth checks and input validation yourself in every action
A Server Action's arguments and return value must be serializable
After a mutation, always call revalidatePath/revalidateTag, otherwise users see stale data

the directive that turns a function into a Server Action

nextjs-deployment.desc: Vercel is the default deployment platform (built by the creators of Next.js). To self-host, use standalone output mode with Docker. The Edge Runtime runs middleware and API routes on edge (CDN) nodes for low latency. Static export works for fully static sites.
nextjs-deployment.q: What is the difference between deploying on Vercel and self-hosting with Docker? What is the Edge Runtime?
nextjs-deployment.qsub: How do you configure Next.js in a monorepo? What is standalone output mode?
nextjs-deployment.what:
Definition: You can deploy Next.js in several ways:

  • Vercel — zero configuration, and every feature (ISR, image optimization, edge) works
  • Docker / self-hosting — output: 'standalone' produces a small image
  • Static export — output: 'export', but SSR, ISR and API routes are all unavailable

Edge vs Node: Edge is fast and runs close to the user, but many Node APIs (fs, parts of crypto, most DB drivers) don't run there.
nextjs-deployment.why: Self-hosting trips people up because ISR needs a persistent filesystem, image optimization needs sharp, and the cache isn't shared across multiple instances. Knowing this up front helps you design the architecture correctly.

The Edge runtime reduces latency worldwide
A static export is nearly free to host on a CDN
cons: Self-hosting takes extra work for ISR and image optimization
Many libraries don't run in the Edge runtime
Some features have limited support outside Vercel
gotchas: NEXT_PUBLIC_ variables are exposed in the browser, so never put secrets in them
Env variables are inlined at build time, so changing them requires a rebuild
Database clients like Prisma often don't run in the Edge runtime, so check first

react-router.qsub: What is the difference between loaders and useEffect for data fetching? How do nested routes work with outlets?
react-router.what:
Definition: React Router is the standard routing library for SPAs. Since v6.4 it includes data APIs: loader (fetch data before rendering), action (handle form submissions) and errorElement (a route-level error boundary).

This removes the "render, then fetch" waterfall, because data and code load in parallel.
react-router.why: The old pattern: render the component, run useEffect, fetch, show a spinner, then show data. With nested routes this creates a waterfall, since the child starts loading only after the parent finishes. With loaders, the router runs the loaders of all matching routes in parallel, so the data is ready before rendering.

Route-level error boundaries are built in
Nested layouts feel natural
cons: Many breaking changes between v5, v6 and the data APIs
Tutorials are often written for older versions
SSR needs separate setup (Remix)
gotchas: For nested routes, the parent must render <Outlet />, otherwise the child won't appear
In a loader, throw a Response (not an Error) so you get the correct status code
v6 has no "exact" prop; matching is exact by default

react-forms.q: When would you choose uncontrolled over controlled components? What are the performance implications?
react-forms.qsub: How does React Hook Form achieve its performance? What is the difference between Formik and React Hook Form?
react-forms.what:
Definition: There are three common ways to build a form:

  • Controlled with useState — fine for small forms (1-3 fields)
  • React Hook Form — uncontrolled inputs with refs, so there is no re-render on every keystroke. The default choice for large forms.
  • Formik — older and based on controlled inputs. RHF is the better pick for new projects.
react-forms.why:
A controlled form with 30 fields re-renders the whole form on every keystroke, so typing feels laggy. RHF keeps inputs uncontrolled and reads values through refs, so nothing re-renders while typing. It re-renders only when an error appears or on submit.

And if you define the schema once with zod, you get both the type and the validation from one place.
pros: No re-renders while typing, so even large forms stay fast
Validation and the TypeScript type come from one zod schema
Error messages, touched and dirty state are built in
cons: Custom components must be wrapped in Controller
The uncontrolled-input mental model takes getting used to
Dependent fields (where one field depends on another) are a bit tricky
gotchas: You must spread {...register("x")}; passing only the name won't work
Use Controller for controlled components like MUI/Radix
Provide defaultValues, otherwise you get an "uncontrolled to controlled" warning

error-boundaries-eco.what:
Definition: A plain class-based boundary only catches errors; it has no way to reset. In practice you also need a retry button, an automatic reset when the route changes, and error logging.

The react-error-boundary library provides all of this through onReset, resetKeys, and the useErrorBoundary hook (which forwards async errors to the boundary).
error-boundaries-eco.why: Async errors are the biggest gap. If a fetch fails, the boundary doesn't catch it, so you'd have to store it in state and render it yourself. With useErrorBoundary().showBoundary(err) you can send that error to the boundary and keep error handling in one place.

Async errors are handled in the same place

prop-types-defaults.qsub: How do you implement the callback ref pattern? What is the difference between useRef and callback refs?
prop-types-defaults.what:
Definition: Three legacy topics that still come up in interviews:

  • PropTypes — runtime prop type checking. Largely redundant next to TypeScript, and no longer checked in React 19.
  • defaultProps — removed for function components in React 19. Use JS default parameters instead.
  • Callback ref — still useful, and React 19 also lets it return a cleanup function.
prop-types-defaults.why: It matters for three reasons: (a) you'll meet these in legacy codebases, (b) interviewers ask "PropTypes vs TypeScript", and (c) a callback ref is still a real tool when you need to act when a node mounts or unmounts. useRef can't do this, because changing a ref doesn't notify you.
pros: A callback ref lets you act reliably on mount and unmount
Default parameters are cleaner and type-safe compared to PropTypes
TypeScript catches issues at compile time, with zero runtime cost
cons: PropTypes duplicates the checking TypeScript already does
An inline callback ref runs on every render unless memoized
defaultProps still works in class components, which causes confusion
gotchas: React 19 removed PropTypes checking and defaultProps for function components
Wrap the callback ref in useCallback, otherwise it is called twice on every render, first with null and then with the node
TypeScript is compile-time only and doesn't validate API data; for that you need something like Zod

the old way to give props default values
passing a function instead of a ref object, so you can run code on mount/unmount
